cards.text: Understand the two main parts of Proposition 19, moving with an existing taxable value and reassessment rules for inherited homes.California Proposition 19 changes how eligible homeowners transfer a home’s taxable value when they move, and how some inherited family homes qualify for reassessment relief. These are different provisions with different requirements, so a benefit available when selling and buying a home does not automatically apply to an inheritance.

cards.text: Before buying or selling a California condo, understand balcony inspections, special assessments, HOA reserves, insurance, and lender project reviews.California’s SB 326 balcony inspection requirements can reveal repairs that an HOA’s reserves cannot cover. Those costs may become special assessments for owners. Combined with condo lending changes and insurance requirements, the association’s condition and financial health deserve as much attention as the unit itself.
cards.title: California’s Condo Crisis: What SB 326 Means for Buyers and Sellers in 2026

cards.text: Preparing your home, support system, and finances for parenthood in your forties.Having children in your forties can bring joy, questions, and a different set of priorities. There is no single timetable that makes a family complete. If you are considering pregnancy, an early conversation with your obstetrician–gynecologist can help you understand your own health and options. Alongside that conversation, think about the support, time, and home environment that would make daily family life work.
cards.title: Having Children in Your 40s

cards.text: Understanding your workplace retirement plan while balancing today’s expenses and tomorrow’s home goals.A 401(k) is a workplace retirement plan that can help you prepare for life beyond your working years. It deserves a place in your financial plan alongside housing, current bills, and emergency savings. Start by understanding what your employer’s plan offers and how its contributions fit your budget.
cards.title: 401K Matters

cards.text: A compassionate space to reflect, care for yourself, and consider your next chapter without pressure.Sometimes the hardest part is not making the decision. It is admitting you are even asking the question. You may still love your partner. You may remember what was good. You may be tired, afraid, angry, hopeful, or all of those things at once.
cards.title: Is It Time for a Divorce? Finding Clarity Without Rushing Your Heart

cards.text: Why assigning every dollar a job can strengthen savings and help you plan for what matters.A budget is not a restriction on your future. It is a way of choosing it. When you decide where your income goes before the month begins, you make room for the things that matter—your bills, your goals, your peace of mind, and even the things you enjoy.
cards.title: The Power of a Budget: Give Every Dollar a Purpose

cards.text: Comparing Studio City and Valley Village? Look at price, neighborhood feel, homes, dining, transportation, and what daily life may feel like in each area.If you are choosing between Studio City and Valley Village, budget may narrow the decision before anything else does. Dominique’s city pages, with market data current as of August 2026, place Studio City’s median home value at approximately $1.8 million to $1.9 million, while Valley Village is approximately $1.1 million to $1.14 million.
cards.title: Studio City or Valley Village, Which One Should I Choose?

cards.title: Coffee or Tea?

cards.text: The Dodgers are chasing a third straight World Series title. Here is what makes the 2026 run historic, what stands in the way, and why Los Angeles is locked in again this October.The Dodgers are not simply trying to win another World Series. They are trying to become the first Major League team since the 1998 through 2000 Yankees to win three championships in a row. Los Angeles entered October as the back to back defending champion, and no National League team has completed a World Series threepeat.
cards.title: Can the Dodgers Do a Threepeat?

cards.text: SoFi Stadium has a packed 2026 NFL calendar. Check which visiting teams are coming to Los Angeles for Rams and Chargers home games this season.SoFi Stadium is home to both the Rams and Chargers, which means Southern California gets a long list of visiting NFL teams every season. If you follow a team outside Los Angeles, this is the part of the schedule worth checking.
cards.title: Football Season Is Back, Does Your Team Play at SoFi This Year?

Within FBS, schools are grouped into conferences.
cards.title: The Different Leagues of College Football

cards.text: From sunset views and special occasion dining to neighborhood favorites and intimate tasting menus, the San Fernando Valley has plenty of places worth putting on your list.One of the best things about living in the San Fernando Valley is that a good meal rarely requires leaving the Valley. You can plan a special dinner with a view, sit down for a tasting menu, grab a relaxed neighborhood meal, or meet friends somewhere lively without making the night about a long drive across Los Angeles. The Valley is spread out, so the easiest way to explore it is to think about the kind of experience you want first, then choose the neighborhood.
cards.title: Places to Eat in the San Fernando Valley

cards.text: There's no universal right answer to this, since it depends on where a couple is in their relationship, their finances, and how much legal complexity they're comfortable navigating before a wedding takes place.
cards.title: Choosing a Home Purchase Timeline Around Marriage

cards.text: Unmarried buyers can choose a title arrangement that reflects their intended ownership, contributions, and inheritance wishes. The title choice is separate from the mortgage application and should be reviewed with an attorney before the deed is recorded.
cards.title: Choosing Home Title for Unmarried Buyers

cards.text: You do not need to merge every account before buying a home together. You do need a clear understanding of purchase contributions, ongoing payments, savings, and the lender’s documentation requirements.
cards.title: Managing Shared Finances Before Buying a Home Together

cards.text: If you divorce later, the house may be kept by one person, sold, or handled another way under the divorce agreement and applicable property law. Buying a home together before or during marriage means thinking ahead to a scenario neither partner wants to imagine, what happens to the house if the marriage ends.
cards.title: Understanding a Shared Home if the Marriage Later Ends

cards.text: Two people may be able to buy together with different credit profiles, but the financing options depend on how the lender evaluates each borrower. A joint application and an application by one borrower can produce different results and different ownership considerations.
cards.title: Joint Home Buying When Only One Partner Has Strong Credit

cards.text: Buying together may suit a couple with a lasting location plan, suitable financing, and a clear agreement about the home’s responsibilities. Continuing to rent can provide flexibility while work, finances, or shared priorities are still changing.
cards.title: Comparing Buying and Renting While Settling Into Married Life

cards.text: Newlyweds can still buy a home with student loan debt by choosing a payment and price range that work after the lender counts the required debt payments. Combining two incomes as a newly married couple can help offset the impact of student loan debt on affordability, but it requires understanding exactly how that debt factors into mortgage qualification.
cards.title: Home Buying for Newlyweds With Student Loan Debt

cards.text: A prenuptial agreement can help clarify property and financial expectations before marriage, including a planned home purchase. Whether it is appropriate and enforceable requires advice from qualified attorneys rather than a real estate recommendation.
cards.title: Prenuptial Agreements and Buying a Home Together

cards.text: A good starter home is one you can comfortably afford now and live in long enough to make the purchase worthwhile, without needing it to be your forever home. A starter home doesn't need to be a couple's forever home, but choosing well still requires thinking beyond just the immediate present.
cards.title: Choosing a Starter Home as a Newly Married Couple

cards.text: You do not have to be married to apply for a joint mortgage. Each applicant still needs to meet the lender’s requirements, and a separate ownership agreement can clarify contributions and responsibilities between unmarried buyers.
cards.title: Joint Mortgage Qualification for Unmarried Buyers

cards.text: Put both goals on one cash flow plan. Compare the wedding budget, cash needed to buy, emergency savings, and the monthly payment you can handle after the wedding so one goal does not weaken the other.
cards.title: Comparing a Home Purchase Before and After the Wedding

cards.text: A prior mortgage can affect the debt used for qualification and the cash available for the next purchase. A lender can compare the outcome if the existing home is kept, sold, or rented before you make an offer.
cards.title: Buying Together When One Spouse Already Has a Mortgage

cards.text: You may still be able to buy together. The lender will consider both borrowers’ income, debts, credit, and available cash, so compare joint and single borrower scenarios before deciding how to apply.
cards.title: Buying Together With Different Credit Scores or Debts

cards.text: Married couples may use both incomes for a joint mortgage when the lender can document and accept them under the selected program. The lender also reviews debts, credit, assets, and the property, so two incomes do not automatically mean approval.
cards.title: Using Both Spouses’ Incomes for a Home Purchase

cards.text: Start with the people who will live there and the routines the home must support: bedrooms, privacy, work or school needs, storage, transportation, outdoor space, and the monthly cost. A larger home is useful only if it solves the household’s real day to day needs.
cards.title: Choosing a Home When Combining Households

cards.text: Compare the cost of moving twice with the cost of buying for the next stage now. The best choice depends on how certain your timing, location, budget, and space needs are, not only on the number of bedrooms.
cards.title: Comparing a Starter Home With a Home for a Growing Family

cards.text: Being named on the title generally means you have an ownership interest in the property. Not being named on the mortgage loan generally means you are not one of the borrowers personally responsible for making the loan payments, although the lender’s lien can still affect the property.
cards.title: Understanding Home Title Without Being on the Mortgage

cards.text: Title and the mortgage do different things: title reflects ownership, while the mortgage identifies who owes the lender. Do not treat adding a spouse to title as a routine form; understand the ownership, lending, and tax consequences first.
cards.title: Considering Adding a Spouse to Your Home’s Title

cards.text: Buying tends to make more sense when your income, location, savings, and expected time in the area are stable enough to justify the upfront and ongoing costs. Compare those costs with a realistic rental alternative before deciding.
cards.title: Comparing Renting and Buying as Newlyweds

cards.text: Getting married does not create a deadline to buy a house. Buying afterward can make sense when your shared budget, savings, location, and expected time in the home support the purchase. Renting longer is a useful option if those decisions are still unsettled.
cards.title: Buying a Home Together Before Marriage

cards.text: You do not automatically have to sell both homes. Compare each property's equity, mortgage, rental potential, tax consequences and how much cash you need for the next purchase before deciding what to keep or sell.
cards.title: Combining Households When Both Partners Own Homes

cards.text: Think beyond one extra bedroom. Prioritize the space, storage, commute, childcare routine, outdoor needs, and monthly payment that will support your family for the years you expect to stay.
cards.title: Planning a Home Purchase for a Growing Family

cards.text: In California, a home owned before marriage generally begins as separate property. That starting point does not settle every later question: changes to title, agreements, and the use of marital funds can affect the analysis. Review the history before adding a name, selling, or assuming how the equity belongs to each spouse.
cards.title: Using Equity From a Home Owned Before Marriage

cards.text: Option 1: Live in the home your fiancé already owns. This can be the simpler choice when the home, payment, location, and ownership arrangement work for both of you.
cards.title: Considering a Partner’s Existing Home and a Joint Purchase

cards.text: Start with a payment that leaves room for savings, childcare, debt, repairs, taxes, insurance, and everyday life. That gives you a usable price range instead of confusing a lender’s maximum approval with a comfortable budget.
cards.title: Finding a Comfortable Home Purchase Range as a Couple

cards.text: You do not need to merge every account before buying a home together. You do need a clear understanding of purchase contributions, ongoing payments, savings, and the lender’s documentation requirements.
cards.title: Managing Shared Finances Before Buying a Home Together

cards.text: If you divorce later, the house may be kept by one person, sold, or handled another way under the divorce agreement and applicable property law. Buying a home together before or during marriage means thinking ahead to a scenario neither partner wants to imagine, what happens to the house if the marriage ends.
cards.title: Understanding a Shared Home if the Marriage Later Ends

cards.text: Two people may be able to buy together with different credit profiles, but the financing options depend on how the lender evaluates each borrower. A joint application and an application by one borrower can produce different results and different ownership considerations.
cards.title: Joint Home Buying When Only One Partner Has Strong Credit

cards.text: Buying together may suit a couple with a lasting location plan, suitable financing, and a clear agreement about the home’s responsibilities. Continuing to rent can provide flexibility while work, finances, or shared priorities are still changing.
cards.title: Comparing Buying and Renting While Settling Into Married Life

cards.text: Newlyweds can still buy a home with student loan debt by choosing a payment and price range that work after the lender counts the required debt payments. Combining two incomes as a newly married couple can help offset the impact of student loan debt on affordability, but it requires understanding exactly how that debt factors into mortgage qualification.
cards.title: Home Buying for Newlyweds With Student Loan Debt

cards.text: A prenuptial agreement can help clarify property and financial expectations before marriage, including a planned home purchase. Whether it is appropriate and enforceable requires advice from qualified attorneys rather than a real estate recommendation.
cards.title: Prenuptial Agreements and Buying a Home Together

cards.text: A good starter home is one you can comfortably afford now and live in long enough to make the purchase worthwhile, without needing it to be your forever home. A starter home doesn't need to be a couple's forever home, but choosing well still requires thinking beyond just the immediate present.
cards.title: Choosing a Starter Home as a Newly Married Couple

cards.text: You do not have to be married to apply for a joint mortgage. Each applicant still needs to meet the lender’s requirements, and a separate ownership agreement can clarify contributions and responsibilities between unmarried buyers.
cards.title: Joint Mortgage Qualification for Unmarried Buyers

cards.text: Put both goals on one cash flow plan. Compare the wedding budget, cash needed to buy, emergency savings, and the monthly payment you can handle after the wedding so one goal does not weaken the other.
cards.title: Comparing a Home Purchase Before and After the Wedding

cards.text: A prior mortgage can affect the debt used for qualification and the cash available for the next purchase. A lender can compare the outcome if the existing home is kept, sold, or rented before you make an offer.
cards.title: Buying Together When One Spouse Already Has a Mortgage

cards.text: You may still be able to buy together. The lender will consider both borrowers’ income, debts, credit, and available cash, so compare joint and single borrower scenarios before deciding how to apply.
cards.title: Buying Together With Different Credit Scores or Debts

cards.text: Married couples may use both incomes for a joint mortgage when the lender can document and accept them under the selected program. The lender also reviews debts, credit, assets, and the property, so two incomes do not automatically mean approval.
cards.title: Using Both Spouses’ Incomes for a Home Purchase

cards.text: Start with the people who will live there and the routines the home must support: bedrooms, privacy, work or school needs, storage, transportation, outdoor space, and the monthly cost. A larger home is useful only if it solves the household’s real day to day needs.
cards.title: Choosing a Home When Combining Households

cards.text: Compare the cost of moving twice with the cost of buying for the next stage now. The best choice depends on how certain your timing, location, budget, and space needs are, not only on the number of bedrooms.
cards.title: Comparing a Starter Home With a Home for a Growing Family

cards.text: Being named on the title generally means you have an ownership interest in the property. Not being named on the mortgage loan generally means you are not one of the borrowers personally responsible for making the loan payments, although the lender’s lien can still affect the property.
cards.title: Understanding Home Title Without Being on the Mortgage

cards.text: Title and the mortgage do different things: title reflects ownership, while the mortgage identifies who owes the lender. Do not treat adding a spouse to title as a routine form; understand the ownership, lending, and tax consequences first.
cards.title: Considering Adding a Spouse to Your Home’s Title

cards.text: Buying tends to make more sense when your income, location, savings, and expected time in the area are stable enough to justify the upfront and ongoing costs. Compare those costs with a realistic rental alternative before deciding.
cards.title: Comparing Renting and Buying as Newlyweds

cards.text: Getting married does not create a deadline to buy a house. Buying afterward can make sense when your shared budget, savings, location, and expected time in the home support the purchase. Renting longer is a useful option if those decisions are still unsettled.
cards.title: Buying a Home Together Before Marriage

cards.text: You do not automatically have to sell both homes. Compare each property's equity, mortgage, rental potential, tax consequences and how much cash you need for the next purchase before deciding what to keep or sell.
cards.title: Combining Households When Both Partners Own Homes

cards.text: Think beyond one extra bedroom. Prioritize the space, storage, commute, childcare routine, outdoor needs, and monthly payment that will support your family for the years you expect to stay.
cards.title: Planning a Home Purchase for a Growing Family

cards.text: In California, a home owned before marriage generally begins as separate property. That starting point does not settle every later question: changes to title, agreements, and the use of marital funds can affect the analysis. Review the history before adding a name, selling, or assuming how the equity belongs to each spouse.
cards.title: Using Equity From a Home Owned Before Marriage

cards.text: Option 1: Live in the home your fiancé already owns. This can be the simpler choice when the home, payment, location, and ownership arrangement work for both of you.
cards.title: Considering a Partner’s Existing Home and a Joint Purchase

cards.text: Start with a payment that leaves room for savings, childcare, debt, repairs, taxes, insurance, and everyday life. That gives you a usable price range instead of confusing a lender’s maximum approval with a comfortable budget.
cards.title: Finding a Comfortable Home Purchase Range as a Couple

Compare the wedding budget, cash needed to buy, emergency savings, and the monthly payment you can handle after the wedding so one goal does not weaken the other.Read MoreLife ChangesBuying Together When One Spouse Already Has a MortgageA prior mortgage can affect the debt used for qualification and the cash available for the next purchase. A lender can compare the outcome if the existing home is kept, sold, or rented before you make an offer.Read MoreLife ChangesBuying Together With Different Credit Scores or DebtsYou may still be able to buy together. The lender will consider both borrowers’ income, debts, credit, and available cash, so compare joint and single borrower scenarios before deciding how to apply.Read MoreLife ChangesUsing Both Spouses’ Incomes for a Home PurchaseMarried couples may use both incomes for a joint mortgage when the lender can document and accept them under the selected program. The lender also reviews debts, credit, assets, and the property, so two incomes do not automatically mean approval.Read MoreLife ChangesChoosing a Home When Combining HouseholdsStart with the people who will live there and the routines the home must support: bedrooms, privacy, work or school needs, storage, transportation, outdoor space, and the monthly cost. A larger home is useful only if it solves the household’s real day to day needs.Read MoreLife ChangesComparing a Starter Home With a Home for a Growing FamilyCompare the cost of moving twice with the cost of buying for the next stage now. The best choice depends on how certain your timing, location, budget, and space needs are, not only on the number of bedrooms.Read MoreLife ChangesUnderstanding Home Title Without Being on the MortgageBeing named on the title generally means you have an ownership interest in the property. Not being named on the mortgage loan generally means you are not one of the borrowers personally responsible for making the loan payments, although the lender’s lien can still affect the property.Read MoreLife ChangesConsidering Adding a Spouse to Your Home’s TitleTitle and the mortgage do different things: title reflects ownership, while the mortgage identifies who owes the lender. Do not treat adding a spouse to title as a routine form; understand the ownership, lending, and tax consequences first.Read MoreLife ChangesComparing Renting and Buying as NewlywedsBuying tends to make more sense when your income, location, savings, and expected time in the area are stable enough to justify the upfront and ongoing costs. Compare those costs with a realistic rental alternative before deciding.Read MoreLife ChangesBuying a Home Together Before MarriageGetting married does not create a deadline to buy a house. Buying afterward can make sense when your shared budget, savings, location, and expected time in the home support the purchase. Renting longer is a useful option if those decisions are still unsettled.Read MoreLife ChangesCombining Households When Both Partners Own HomesYou do not automatically have to sell both homes. Compare each property's equity, mortgage, rental potential, tax consequences and how much cash you need for the next purchase before deciding what to keep or sell.Read MoreLife ChangesPlanning a Home Purchase for a Growing FamilyThink beyond one extra bedroom. Prioritize the space, storage, commute, childcare routine, outdoor needs, and monthly payment that will support your family for the years you expect to stay.Read MoreLife ChangesUsing Equity From a Home Owned Before MarriageIn California, a home owned before marriage generally begins as separate property. That starting point does not settle every later question: changes to title, agreements, and the use of marital funds can affect the analysis. Review the history before adding a name, selling, or assuming how the equity belongs to each spouse.Read MoreLife ChangesConsidering a Partner’s Existing Home and a Joint PurchaseOption 1: Live in the home your fiancé already owns. This can be the simpler choice when the home, payment, location, and ownership arrangement work for both of you.Read MoreLife ChangesFinding a Comfortable Home Purchase Range as a CoupleStart with a payment that leaves room for savings, childcare, debt, repairs, taxes, insurance, and everyday life. That gives you a usable price range instead of confusing a lender’s maximum approval with a comfortable budget.Read MoreContact Dominique
